title: Trigonometric Laws: Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
learningObjective: Use the law of sines and/or the law of cosines to solve non-right triangles.

faqs.question: What is the Law of Sines, and what does it actually say?
faqs.answer:
The Law of Sines says that in any triangle — right or not — the ratio of a side's length to the sine of its opposite angle is the same for all three sides.
Formula

\[ \dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C} \]

You only ever need to set ONE fraction equal to another — not all three at once.

Each side is paired with the angle directly across from it — same color: side a ↔ angle A, side b ↔ angle B, side c ↔ angle C. The Law of Sines says each pair has the same ratio.

faqs.question: When can I use the Law of Sines to solve a triangle?
faqs.answer: The Law of Sines works whenever you have a complete opposite pair — an angle and the side directly across from it — plus one more piece of information. In practice, that means it applies to AAS and ASA triangles (two angles and a side) and to SSA triangles (two sides and a non-included angle) — though SSA comes with a complication of its own (faq-5).

faqs.question: What is the Law of Cosines, and how is it different from the Pythagorean Theorem?
faqs.answer:
The Law of Cosines relates all three sides of ANY triangle to the cosine of one included angle — it's a generalized version of the Pythagorean Theorem that works even when there's no right angle.
Formula

\[ a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A \]

If angle A happens to be 90°, then \( \cos A = 0 \), and the whole last term disappears — leaving exactly \( a^2=b^2+c^2 \), the Pythagorean Theorem. The Pythagorean Theorem is really just a special case of this more general law.

Law of Cosines setup: sides b and c (orange) are the two sides that form angle A, and side a (teal) is the side across from A: a² = b² + c² − 2bc·cos A.

faqs.question: When do I need the Law of Cosines instead of the Law of Sines?
faqs.answer: Use the Law of Cosines whenever you DON'T have a complete opposite pair (an angle and its directly-across side) to work with — specifically for SAS triangles (two sides and the included angle) and SSS triangles (all three sides, no angles at all). The Law of Sines simply has no way to get started in either of those situations.

faqs.question: What is the Ambiguous Case, and why does it only happen with the Law of Sines?
faqs.answer:
The Ambiguous Case happens specifically with SSA triangles (two sides and a non-included angle), where the given information can produce zero, one, or two valid triangles — not always exactly one. This happens because sine is positive in both Quadrant I and Quadrant II (TR5), so when you solve for an angle using the Law of Sines, there are genuinely two different angle values that could both make the sine ratio true — and you have to check whether one, both, or neither actually forms a valid triangle. The Law of Cosines never has this problem, since it always produces a unique answer.

Swinging side a (dashed circle) crosses the baseline twice — two different triangles both satisfy the same given information.

faqs.question: What do AAS, ASA, SSA, SAS, and SSS mean, and why does the letter order matter?
faqs.answer:
Each letter combination describes which three pieces of a triangle you're given, in the order you'd encounter them going around the triangle — A for a known angle, S for a known side. The ORDER matters because it tells you whether a given angle sits between two known sides or not.

The same triangle, five ways: orange marks the three pieces you're given (sides thick, angles as arcs). Which pieces you have — and in what order around the triangle — decides which law to use.

Summary

AAS / ASA — two angles + a side → Law of Sines (no ambiguity)

SSA — two sides + non-included angle → Law of Sines (Ambiguous Case!)

SAS — two sides + included angle → Law of Cosines

SSS — three sides, no angles → Law of Cosines

faqs.question: How do I solve a triangle when I'm given two angles and a side (AAS or ASA)?
faqs.answer:
Find the third angle first by subtracting the two known angles from 180°, then use the Law of Sines twice — once for each remaining missing side.

Triangle ABC, true to scale: angles A = 40° and C = 75° and side a = 12 are known (navy). Angle B and sides b and c (orange) are what we solve for.

Worked Example

Triangle ABC: \( A=40° \), \( C=75° \), \( a=12 \). Find B, b, and c.

\( B=180°-40°-75°=65° \)

\( \dfrac{12}{\sin 40°}=\dfrac{b}{\sin 65°} \) → \( b\approx 16.9 \)

\( \dfrac{12}{\sin 40°}=\dfrac{c}{\sin 75°} \) → \( c\approx 18.0 \)

faqs.question: How do I set up the Law of Sines proportion correctly?
faqs.answer:
Match each side with the angle DIRECTLY ACROSS from it — never a side with an adjacent angle. Write your proportion using only the one complete opposite pair you already know, plus the pair you're solving for.

Match across the triangle: the known pair is angle B with side b (navy). We're solving for side c, so its partner is the angle across from it, angle C (orange): b / sin B = c / sin C.

Worked Example

Known: angle \( B \) and its opposite side \( b \). Solving for side \( c \), opposite angle \( C \).

\( \dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C} \)

faqs.question: How do I know how many triangles exist in an SSA (Ambiguous Case) situation?
faqs.answer:
Solve for the unknown angle using the Law of Sines as usual, but check the result BEFORE moving on. If the sine value comes out greater than 1, no triangle exists at all — sine can never exceed 1 (TR5). If it's a valid sine value, you get one candidate angle immediately, and there's always a second candidate angle (180° minus the first) to check as well — see faq-11 for how to test whether that second candidate actually works.

Given angle A, side b, and the swinging side a (dashed circle, radius a): compare a with the height h = b·sin A. The circle either misses the baseline, touches it once, crosses it twice, or crosses it once in front of A and once behind it.

Worked Example — No Solution

\( B=84° \), \( a=18 \), \( b=9 \): \( \dfrac{18}{\sin A}=\dfrac{9}{\sin 84°} \) → \( \sin A \approx 1.99 \)

Since sine can never exceed 1, no triangle exists.

faqs.question: How do I find both possible triangles when there are two solutions in the Ambiguous Case?
faqs.answer:
Solve for the first (acute) candidate angle using the inverse sine as usual, then find the second candidate by subtracting that result from 180°. Check that the second candidate is actually valid (faq-11), and if so, solve the REST of both triangles completely and separately — they'll have different remaining angles and sides.

Angle B = 45°, side a = 28, side b = 27 (true to scale). Side b can swing to either of two spots on the baseline, giving two genuinely different triangles that share angle B and sides a and b.

Worked Example

\( B=45° \), \( a=28 \), \( b=27 \): first candidate \( A\approx 47.2° \), second candidate \( A\approx 132.8° \)

Both are valid here, producing two completely different triangles.

faqs.question: How do I know when a second candidate triangle from the Ambiguous Case is actually invalid?
faqs.answer:
Add the second candidate angle to the OTHER angle you already knew. If that sum is 180° or more, the third angle would have to be zero or negative — which is impossible — so that second triangle doesn't actually exist.

A triangle's angles must fit inside 180°. Once the two angles already add past 180°, there is no room for the third — so that candidate triangle is impossible.

Worked Example

Known angle \( C=145° \), second candidate \( B\approx 156° \)

\( 145°+156°=301° \), already over 180° — this second triangle is impossible.

faqs.question: How do I use the Law of Cosines to find a missing side when given two sides and the included angle (SAS)?
faqs.answer:
Plug the two known sides and the included angle directly into the Law of Cosines formula, matching the missing side to the angle between the two known sides.

SAS, true to scale: sides b = 14 and c = 7 and the angle between them, A = 70° (navy). The side across from A (orange) comes out to about 13.3.

Worked Example

Triangle ABC: \( A=70° \), \( b=14 \), \( c=7 \). Find side a.

\( a^2=14^2+7^2-2(14)(7)\cos 70° \)

\( a^2\approx 196+49-67.06\approx 177.9 \) → \( a\approx 13.3 \)

faqs.question: How do I use the Law of Cosines to find a missing angle when given all three sides (SSS)?
faqs.answer:
Rearrange the Law of Cosines to isolate the cosine term, plug in all three known sides, then apply the inverse cosine to solve for the angle itself.

SSS, true to scale: all three sides are known (navy) and angle C (orange) is the unknown. Notice this one happens to be a right triangle (8² + 6² = 10²) — so C turns out to be exactly 90°.

Worked Example

Triangle with sides \( a=8 \), \( b=6 \), \( c=10 \). Find angle C.

\( c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C \) → \( \cos C=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab} \)

\( \cos C=\dfrac{64+36-100}{96}=0 \) → \( C=\arccos(0)=90° \)

faqs.question: Once I've found one angle in an SSS or SAS triangle, how do I find the other two?
faqs.answer: Once you have at least one full opposite pair (an angle and its matching side), it's usually fastest to switch over to the Law of Sines for the second angle — then find the third angle by subtracting the first two from 180°. You can also use the Law of Cosines a second time if you prefer to stay consistent, but the Law of Sines is typically quicker once you have one angle to work with.

faqs.question: How do I decide which law to use — Law of Sines or Law of Cosines — just by looking at what I'm given?
faqs.answer:
Check whether you have a complete opposite pair (an angle and the side directly across from it) among your given information. If yes, use the Law of Sines. If no complete opposite pair exists — meaning you only have SAS or SSS information — use the Law of Cosines instead, since it's the only tool that can get started without one.

A quick decision guide: the question is always whether you already hold a complete opposite pair — an angle and the side directly across from it.

faqs.question: How does this section connect to TE4's right-triangle solving?
faqs.answer: TE4's tools — SOH-CAH-TOA and the Pythagorean Theorem — only work when a triangle has a right angle. This section extends triangle-solving to EVERY triangle, right or not, using two more general laws that still rely on the same underlying trig ratios TE4 introduced. In fact, faq-3 shows the Pythagorean Theorem is just the Law of Cosines with a 90° angle plugged in — TE4 was always a special case of what you're learning here.

faqs.question: How does the Ambiguous Case connect to TR5's quadrant sign ideas?
faqs.answer:
The entire reason the Ambiguous Case exists is TR5's observation that sine is positive in both Quadrant I and Quadrant II — meaning two different angles between 0° and 180° can share the exact same sine value. Solving a triangle with the Law of Sines runs directly into that same ambiguity, which is why you always have to check both candidate angles rather than assuming there's only one answer.

On the unit circle, the angles B and 180° − B land at exactly the same height — so they have the same sine. When the Law of Sines hands you a sine value, both angles are candidates for the triangle.

faqs.question: Why do the Law of Sines and Law of Cosines matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Surveying, navigation, and engineering all depend on solving triangles that aren't conveniently right triangles — measuring distances across terrain you can't directly walk across, calculating forces at odd angles, or triangulating a position using bearings to two known landmarks. These two laws are the standard tools for exactly that kind of real-world triangle, and they reappear constantly in physics and any field involving vectors or forces at an angle.

guided.title: Practice the Law of Sines for AAS/ASA
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve a triangle using the Law of Sines when I'm given two angles and a side. Give me a triangle like this and walk me through finding the third angle first, then using the Law of Sines twice to find the two missing sides. Give me more practice problems and check my work.

guided.title: Master the Ambiguous Case Decision Process
guided.prompt: I'm learning to figure out how many triangles exist in an SSA (Ambiguous Case) situation. Give me a triangle with two sides and a non-included angle, and walk me through the full process: solve for the angle, check if the sine value is valid, find both candidate angles, and check whether the second candidate is actually possible. Give me three more practice problems — one with no solution, one with one solution, and one with two solutions — and check my reasoning each time.

guided.title: Practice the Law of Cosines for SAS and SSS
guided.prompt: I'm learning to use the Law of Cosines. Give me a triangle with two sides and the included angle (SAS), and walk me through finding the missing side. Then give me a triangle with all three sides (SSS) and walk me through finding a missing angle. Give me more practice problems of each type and check my work.

guided.title: Practice Choosing the Right Law
guided.prompt: I sometimes struggle to decide whether to use the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines. Give me several different triangle scenarios — some AAS, some SSA, some SAS, some SSS — and ask me to identify which law I'd use for each one before I actually solve anything. Check my reasoning and help me understand any I got wrong.

guided.title: Connect the Ambiguous Case to TR5
guided.prompt: I've learned that the Ambiguous Case happens because sine is positive in both Quadrant I and Quadrant II, which I first learned about in TR5. Can you help me see this connection concretely — walk me through why solving sin(B) = 0.7, for example, gives two different valid angles between 0° and 180°, and how that directly explains why the Law of Sines can produce two triangles?

stages.desc: Three quick reviews TE5 leans on: triangle labels (TE4), calculator and proportions, and why two angles can share a sine (TR5/PF3). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Label the triangle; angles add to 180°
stops.target: Side \(a\) is across from angle \(A\), \(b\) across from \(B\), \(c\) across from \(C\). The three angles add to \(180^\circ\), and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 48^\circ\) and \(B = 71^\circ\). Find \(C\). Which side is the longest?[[graph:G1q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, A = 48 degrees and B = 71 degrees. Find C. Which side is the longest?
stops.coldA: \(C = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 71^\circ = 61^\circ\). The largest angle is \(B = 71^\circ\), so the longest side is \(b\).[[graph:G1s]]
stops.solution: C = 180 - 48 - 71 = 61 degrees. The largest angle is B = 71, and the longest side is the one across from it: side b.
stops.mistake: Picking the side that touches the largest angle instead of the side across from it.
stops.again: \(A = 112^\circ\), \(C = 25^\circ\). Find \(B\). Which side is longest? Which is shortest?
stops.againA: \(B = 43^\circ\). Longest side \(a\) (across from \(112^\circ\)); shortest side \(c\) (across from \(25^\circ\)).
stops.reflect: How could "longest side across from largest angle" help you catch a wrong answer later?

stops.title: Calculator: degrees, inverse trig, and proportions
stops.target: In degree mode, solve a proportion by cross-multiplying, and undo \(\sin\) or \(\cos\) with \(\sin^{-1}\) or \(\cos^{-1}\).
stops.cold: (1) Solve \(\dfrac{x}{\sin 40^\circ} = \dfrac{12}{\sin 75^\circ}\) to the nearest tenth. (2) Find \(\theta\) if \(\sin\theta = 0.8\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.coldPlain: (1) Solve x / sin 40 degrees = 12 / sin 75 degrees, to the nearest tenth. (2) Find theta if sin theta = 0.8, to the nearest tenth of a degree.
stops.solution: (1) Multiply both sides by sin 40: x = 12 sin 40 / sin 75, about 8.0. (2) theta = sin^(-1)(0.8), about 53.1 degrees.
stops.mistake: Leaving the calculator in radian mode: 12 sin(40)/sin(75) comes out about -23.1, which cannot be a side length.
stops.againA: (1) \(x \approx 4.5\). (2) \(\cos^{-1}(-0.3) \approx 107.5^\circ\) (a negative cosine gives an obtuse angle).
stops.reflect: What is a quick way to check that your calculator is in degree mode before a quiz?

stops.title: Two angles can share a sine
stops.target: Between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), \(\sin\theta = \sin(180^\circ - \theta)\), so an equation \(\sin\theta = k\) (with \(0 < k < 1\)) has two answers. \(\cos\theta = k\) has only one.
stops.cold: For \(0^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ\): (1) solve \(\sin\theta = 0.6\); (2) solve \(\cos\theta = -0.6\). Round to the nearest tenth.
stops.coldPlain: For theta between 0 and 180 degrees: (1) solve sin theta = 0.6; (2) solve cos theta = -0.6. Round to the nearest tenth.
stops.solution: Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, so sin theta = 0.6 gives 36.9 degrees from the calculator and also 180 - 36.9 = 143.1 degrees. Cosine is negative only in Quadrant II on this interval, so cos theta = -0.6 gives only 126.9 degrees.
stops.mistake: Stopping at the calculator answer for sine and missing 180 - theta.
stops.reflect: Why might two different triangles have angles with the same sine? (This is exactly the "ambiguous case" coming up.)

stages.desc: Choose the law, use each law, then handle the ambiguous SSA case.

stops.title: Which law? Look for a matched pair
stops.target: Name what you are given (AAS, ASA, SSA, SAS, SSS) and choose the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines, with a reason.
stops.cold: Which law would you start with, and why? (1) \(A = 40^\circ, B = 65^\circ, c = 10\) (2) \(a = 7, b = 9, C = 52^\circ\) (3) \(a = 5, b = 7, c = 9\) (4) \(A = 30^\circ, a = 6, b = 10\)
stops.coldPlain: Which law would you start with, and why? (1) A = 40, B = 65, c = 10 (2) a = 7, b = 9, C = 52 (3) a = 5, b = 7, c = 9 (4) A = 30, a = 6, b = 10
stops.coldA: (1) ASA: find \(C = 75^\circ\) first, then \(c\) and \(C\) are a matched pair, so Law of Sines. (2) SAS: \(C\) is between \(a\) and \(b\), no matched pair, so Law of Cosines. (3) SSS: no angles, so Law of Cosines. (4) SSA: \(a\) and \(A\) are a matched pair, so Law of Sines, and check for two triangles.
stops.solution: (1) ASA; the third angle C = 75 makes c and C a matched pair, so Law of Sines. (2) SAS; the given angle sits between the two given sides, so there is no matched pair: Law of Cosines. (3) SSS; no angles at all: Law of Cosines. (4) SSA; a and A are a matched pair, so Law of Sines, but this is the ambiguous case, so check for 0, 1, or 2 triangles.
stops.mistake: Choosing a law by memorized letter patterns without checking whether a side and its opposite angle are both known.
stops.again: (1) \(B = 35^\circ, C = 80^\circ, b = 12\) (2) \(b = 8, c = 11, A = 120^\circ\). On a CheckIt the letters may be shuffled, so read which angle is across from which side.
stops.againA: (1) AAS, \(b\) and \(B\) are a matched pair: Law of Sines. (2) SAS, \(A\) is between \(b\) and \(c\): Law of Cosines.
stops.reflect: In your own words, what is a "matched pair," and why does the Law of Sines need one?

stops.title: Law of Sines: AAS and ASA
stops.target: With two angles and a side, find the third angle, then use \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}\) for each missing side.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 40^\circ\), \(B = 65^\circ\), and \(c = 10\). Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).[[graph:T2q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, A = 40 degrees, B = 65 degrees, and c = 10. Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: C = 180 - 40 - 65 = 75, so c = 10 and C = 75 are a matched pair. a = 10 sin 40 / sin 75, about 6.7. b = 10 sin 65 / sin 75, about 9.4.
stops.mistake: Trying to use the Law of Sines before finding C, so there is no complete ratio to set equal.
stops.reflect: Why does AAS or ASA never give two different triangles?

stops.title: Law of Cosines: SAS
stops.target: With two sides and the angle between them, find the third side with \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\). Then find an angle that is not across from the longest side, and finish with the angle sum.
stops.explain:
The Law of Cosines is the Pythagorean Theorem with a correction term for angles that are not \(90^\circ\).

[[graph:PYTH]]
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(a = 7\), \(b = 9\), and \(C = 52^\circ\). Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).[[graph:T3q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, a = 7, b = 9, and C = 52 degrees. Solve the triangle (round to the nearest tenth).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: c^2 = 49 + 81 - 126 cos 52, about 52.43, so c is about 7.2. a = 7 is not the longest side, so A is acute and the Law of Sines is safe: sin A = 7 sin 52 / 7.2, A about 49.6. B = 180 - 52 - 49.6, about 78.4. Keep unrounded values in the calculator between steps.
stops.mistake: Computing (49 + 81 - 126) cos 52 instead of 49 + 81 - (126 cos 52): multiply 2ab by cos C before subtracting.
stops.stretch: In the last problem, why would it be risky to find the \(120^\circ\) angle with the Law of Sines if it had not been given?
stops.stretchA: \(\sin^{-1}\) only returns angles up to \(90^\circ\). Since \(\sin 120^\circ = \sin 60^\circ\), the calculator would report \(60^\circ\). Find the largest angle with the Law of Cosines or the angle sum.
stops.reflect: What does the sign of cos C tell you about the side across from C?

stops.title: Law of Cosines: SSS
stops.target: With three sides, find the largest angle first with \(\cos C = \dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\) (a negative value means obtuse), then the rest.
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(a = 5\), \(b = 7\), \(c = 9\). Solve the triangle (round angles to the nearest tenth).[[graph:T4q]]
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, a = 5, b = 7, c = 9. Solve the triangle (round angles to the nearest tenth).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: The longest side is c = 9, so find C first: cos C = (25 + 49 - 81)/70 = -0.1, C about 95.7 degrees (obtuse). Then sin A = 5 sin C / 9 gives A about 33.6, and B = 180 - C - A, about 50.7.
stops.mistake: Putting the wrong side in the subtracted spot: the side across from the angle you want is the one subtracted.
stops.reflect: Why is "largest angle first" a good habit when you will use the Law of Sines afterward?

stops.title: SSA: zero, one, or two triangles?
stops.target: Given \(A\), \(a\), and \(b\): find \(\sin B = \dfrac{b\sin A}{a}\). If it is more than 1, no triangle. Otherwise test both \(B\) and \(180^\circ - B\): each one counts only if it fits with \(A\) under \(180^\circ\).
stops.explain:
Side \(a\) hangs from \(C\) like a gate. It can swing to land on the base in two places, in one place, or not reach at all.

[[graph:SW]]
stops.solution: (1) sin B = 10 sin 30 / 6, about 0.8333: B is about 56.4 or 123.6, and 30 + 123.6 < 180, so two triangles. (2) sin B = 9 sin 50 / 12, about 0.5745: B is about 35.1 or 144.9, but 50 + 144.9 > 180, so one triangle. (3) sin B = 10 sin 40 / 4, about 1.607, more than 1, so no triangle.
stops.mistake: Writing down only the calculator angle and never testing 180 - B.
stops.againA: (1) \(\sin B \approx 0.8604\), \(B \approx 59.4^\circ\) or \(120.6^\circ\); both work: two triangles. (2) \(\sin B \approx 0.6265\), \(B \approx 38.8^\circ\) works, \(141.2^\circ\) does not (\(110^\circ + 141.2^\circ > 180^\circ\)): one triangle.
stops.reflect: Use the gate picture: why does a short side a sometimes give two triangles and sometimes none?

stops.title: SSA: solve both triangles
stops.target: When there are two triangles, finish each one separately: \(C = 180^\circ - A - B\), then \(c = \dfrac{a\sin C}{\sin A}\).
stops.cold: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 6\), \(b = 10\). Find every possible triangle (round to the nearest tenth).
stops.coldPlain: In triangle ABC, A = 30 degrees, a = 6, b = 10. Find every possible triangle (round to the nearest tenth).
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.solution: sin B = 10 sin 30 / 6, about 0.8333, so B1 is about 56.4 and B2 = 180 - 56.4, about 123.6; both fit with A = 30. Triangle 1: C about 93.6, c = 6 sin C / sin 30, about 12.0. Triangle 2: C about 26.4, c about 5.3.
stops.mistake: Mixing the two triangles, for example using C from triangle 1 to find c in triangle 2.
stops.reflect: How would you show a grader that you checked for a second triangle, even when there is only one?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the TE5 CheckIt: one Law of Cosines triangle, one Law of Sines triangle, and one that may have two solutions.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Solve non-right triangles: state which law you used and why, and check for a second triangle when the case is SSA.
stops.cold:
Solve each triangle. State whether you used the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines and explain your choice. If there may be two solutions, show that you checked and give both when appropriate. Round to the nearest tenth.
(1) \(a = 10\), \(c = 14\), and \(B = 35^\circ\).
(2) \(A = 55^\circ\), \(C = 60^\circ\), and \(b = 12\).
(3) \(C = 40^\circ\), \(c = 7\), and \(a = 10\).
stops.coldPlain: Solve each triangle, state which law and why, and check for two solutions. (1) a = 10, c = 14, B = 35 degrees. (2) A = 55, C = 60 degrees, b = 12. (3) C = 40 degrees, c = 7, a = 10. Round to the nearest tenth.
stops.note: Show which law you used for each missing part and why, and check that the angles add to 180 degrees and the longest side is across from the largest angle.
stops.coldA: (1) Law of Cosines (SAS): \(b \approx 8.2\), \(A \approx 44.6^\circ\), \(C \approx 100.4^\circ\).[[graph:SF1]](2) Law of Sines (ASA): \(B = 65^\circ\), \(a \approx 10.8\), \(c \approx 11.5\).[[graph:SF2]](3) Law of Sines (SSA), two triangles: \(A \approx 66.7^\circ\), \(B \approx 73.3^\circ\), \(b \approx 10.4\); or \(A \approx 113.3^\circ\), \(B \approx 26.7^\circ\), \(b \approx 4.9\).[[graph:SF3]][[graph:SWF]]
stops.solution: (1) SAS, B is between a and c: b^2 = 100 + 196 - 280 cos 35, b about 8.2; sin A = 10 sin 35 / b, A about 44.6; C about 100.4. (2) ASA: B = 65, a = 12 sin 55 / sin 65, about 10.8; c = 12 sin 60 / sin 65, about 11.5. (3) SSA, c and C are a matched pair: sin A = 10 sin 40 / 7, about 0.9183, so A is about 66.7 or 113.3; 40 + 113.3 < 180, so two triangles: B about 73.3 with b about 10.4, or B about 26.7 with b about 4.9.
stops.mistake: In (3), reading the letters as if they were A, a, b: here the matched pair is c and C, and the angle to solve for is A.
stops.againA: (1) Law of Cosines: \(C \approx 88.0^\circ\), \(A \approx 35.7^\circ\), \(B \approx 56.4^\circ\). (2) Law of Sines: \(C = 45^\circ\), \(b \approx 17.8\), \(c \approx 13.4\). (3) Law of Sines: \(\sin A \approx 0.5472\), \(A \approx 33.2^\circ\) (the other option, \(146.8^\circ\), is too big with \(50^\circ\)): one triangle, \(C \approx 96.8^\circ\), \(c \approx 18.1\).
stops.reflect: Which part of TE5 still feels shaky: choosing the law, the Law of Cosines arithmetic, or the ambiguous case?
